```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.2, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
```

An ordinary calibration returns one set of parameters, the best it found. It says nothing about
the other sets that fit nearly as well, or about how far the forecast might be from the truth
because of them. Bayesian calibration returns all of them: a sample of every set consistent
with the record and with what was known before, each in proportion to how well it fits. The
spread of the sample is the uncertainty of the parameters; running its sets gives a band round
the forecast.

# The idea in three parts

1. **The prior** is what was known before looking at the record: that `cmax` is likely to be
   around 250 mm, say, give or take 30%. It may come from experience, from a regional study,
   or from a model of parameters from catchment descriptors.
2. **The likelihood** is how probable the observed flows are if a given set is right. It needs a
   model of the errors.
3. **The posterior** combines the two: sets that fit the record well and are plausible
   beforehand. Where the record pins a parameter down, the record wins; where it cannot, the
   prior keeps the parameter sensible instead of letting it drift to a bound.

# The error model

The likelihood treats the errors on Box-Cox flows ([Counting every error fairly](fair-errors.html))
as running on from one hour to the next: this hour's error is a share `rho` of the last hour's
plus a fresh error. Hourly errors do run on, because a model that is too low at the start of a
recession stays too low for hours. Treating them as independent would count each hour as new
evidence and make the posterior far too sure of itself. `rho` and the size of the fresh errors
are set to their best values for each set.

# The sampler

The posterior cannot be written down; it is sampled. `calibrate_bayes()` uses DREAM(ZS)
(ter Braak and Vrugt, 2008; Vrugt, 2016). Several chains wander through the parameter space. Each
step proposes a jump built from the difference between two past positions, kept in an archive,
and accepts it more readily the better it fits. Built that way, the jumps take the shape of the
posterior itself, which suits the long, curved ridges of hydrological models and needs no
tuning. The first half of every chain is discarded as burn-in.

# An example

The synthetic catchment of the other articles, with a prior on `fc` centred on the truth and a
uniform prior, over its bounds, on `cmax`:

```{r data}
rain <- synthetic_rain("2017-10-01", years = 3, dt = 1, seed = 5)
truth <- modifyList(pdm_presets("standard"), list(area_km2 = 25))
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
forcing <- rain[c("time", "rain", "pet")]
set.seed(8)
flow <- run_pdm(model, forcing[c("rain", "pet")], initial_state(model, 0.5))$output$q_m3s
observed <- flow * exp(rnorm(length(flow), 0, 0.15))
```

```{r bayes}
post <- calibrate_bayes(truth, forcing, observed, lower = c(fc = 0.6, distribution.cmax = 100),
                        upper = c(fc = 1.4, distribution.cmax = 500),
                        priors = list(fc = prior_normal(1, 0.3)), generations = 800,
                        lambda = 0, warmup = 24 * 90, start = "soil", seed = 3)
post
```

Each parameter has its mean, spread and 5%, 50% and 95% points. `rhat` compares the chains:
under about 1.2 for every parameter they have found the same posterior; above it, run more
generations. The power of the Box-Cox transform is 0 here because these errors are proportional
to the flow.

The posterior is narrow: three years of hourly flow pin `fc` down to within a fraction of a per
cent. That is honest about the parameters, given this model and this rain. It says nothing about
errors in the rain itself, which calibrating on the rainfall used operationally deals with. Where
the posterior is still too sure, `temper` below 1 counts the record as worth less: 0.25 treats it
as a quarter of its length.

# Seeing the posterior

The sample is a table of sets; its columns can be plotted like any data.

```{r pairs, fig.height=4}
plot(post$samples$fc, post$samples$distribution.cmax, pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
     col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", 0.4), xlab = "fc", ylab = "cmax (mm)",
     main = "Posterior sets")
points(1, 300, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3)
```

The cross is the truth. A tilted cloud would show the two parameters trading off against each
other, a ridge of equally good sets; a round one, that the record determines each on its own.

# A predictive band

`posterior_band()` runs sets drawn from the posterior. Without the error model the band shows the
parameters' uncertainty alone; with it, the band is where the observed flow should fall.

```{r band}
band <- posterior_band(post, forcing, draws = 50, noise = TRUE)
rows <- which.max(observed) + seq(-72, 120)
plot(forcing$time[rows], observed[rows], type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)",
     main = "The largest flood, with the 90% predictive band")
polygon(c(forcing$time[rows], rev(forcing$time[rows])), c(band$q05[rows], rev(band$q95[rows])),
        col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", 0.25), border = NA)
lines(forcing$time[rows], band$q50[rows], col = "#0072B2", lwd = 1.5)
covered <- mean(observed >= band$q05 & observed <= band$q95, na.rm = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Share of hours inside the 90%% band: %.0f%%\n", 100 * covered))
```

A 90% band should hold about 90% of the observations. Far fewer means the band is too narrow, the
error model too optimistic; far more, too cautious. [Is a probability forecast
honest?](ensemble-verification.html) checks this properly.

# Priors from catchment descriptors

A model of parameters from catchment descriptors, trained on many catchments, predicts each
parameter of a new catchment with a spread. `priors_from_table()` turns its predictions into
priors:

```{r priors}
predicted <- data.frame(parameter = c("distribution.cmax", "fc"),
                        median = c(280, NA), sdlog = c(0.25, NA),
                        mean = c(NA, 1.05), sd = c(NA, 0.1))
priors_from_table(predicted, widen = 1.5)
```

`widen` stretches every spread, to allow for the catchment being one the model has not seen.
With priors like these, a short record calibrates far better than it could alone, and an ungauged
catchment can still be modelled, from the priors only.

# Cautions

- **Check `rhat` every time.** A run that has not converged gives a sample of the wrong thing.
- **The posterior is only as good as the error model.** Choose the Box-Cox power so the errors
  are the same size at every flow, and check the band's coverage.
- **It costs thousands of runs**: chains times generations. On long 15-minute records, a coarser
  step for a first look, or a shorter record, keeps it practical.
